fg.methodology_md:
The **Fear & Greed Index** condenses seven market signals into a single value from **0 (extreme fear)** to **100 (extreme greed)**. It measures not price direction but the *sentiment* behind it — whether the market is driven by fear or complacency.

**Breadth** (across all index members, from the simulation database):

- **Momentum** — the index above/below its SMA125, normalised against its own history.
- **Breadth** — average of % of members above SMA200, % with RSI > 50 and the bullish share (Markov regime).
- **52-week strength** — net new 52-week highs minus lows (via lyHigh/lyLow).

**Volatility & hedging** (macro series):

- **Volatility** — VIX relative to its 1-year range (high VIX = fear).
- **Term structure** — VIX vs. VIX3M; when the curve tips into backwardation, fear rises. Substitutes the classic put/call ratio, which is not available from the data source.
- **Safe haven** — 60-day return of the index minus TLT (Treasuries): when stocks beat bonds, greed prevails.
- **Junk-bond demand** — 60-day return of HYG (high yield) minus LQD (investment grade): tight spreads = risk appetite.

**Normalisation:** each component is normalised **against its own multi-year history** to 0–100 (percentile or z-score) — breadth against the yearly history including the 2020/2022 bear markets, otherwise every bull market would read as "greed" — and then averaged with equal weights.

**Sources:** price/volume data and indicators from the local database (`asset_simulation`, `yf_*`); macro series VIX, VIX3M, TLT, HYG, LQD from the active data provider. The index is a **sentiment gauge, not a buy/sell signal**.

sf.sizing_cap_help: Position size is capital x (avg vola / asset vola) / slots. The factor is unbounded upwards, and the only check is whether cash covers ONE share - so the cash balance can go negative (measured: ZN=F at vola 1.4 against an average of 9.95 gives 142,133 EUR on 100,000 capital with 5 slots). "none" leaves that as it is and keeps older results comparable. "to available cash" caps every buy at the cash on hand including the fee and guarantees a balance >= 0; the price is that whoever buys first gets more. "to volatility factor" clamps the factor to [1/f, f], limiting single-position concentration - but it does NOT guarantee a positive balance, since f x slots can exceed 100%. The setting also applies to Multi Strategies and changes every backtest result.
sf.sizing_factor_max_help: Upper bound of the avg-vola/asset-vola factor; the lower bound is its reciprocal 1/f. f = 2 means no position larger than two slots and none smaller than half a slot. f = 1 is plain equal weighting. Values below 1 are raised to 1, otherwise the lower bound would exceed the upper one.
mt.strategies_help: Which strategies are computed. All of them by default. A deselected strategy is neither simulated nor shown in metrics and tables - the result is a different portfolio, not the same one with less on screen. What gets stored is the deselection, so a newly added strategy runs automatically. Applies to this page only; the nightly signal run still computes all of them.

mt.show_charts_help: On (default): a price chart per name appears below the buy and sell tables once a row is selected. Off: tables only. mt.dedup_help: Off (default): when more than one strategy picks the same asset, several may hold it at the same time. On: only the strategy that bought first keeps it; later buy signals for the same asset are dropped while it is held. That lowers concentration risk but has measurably cost return — doubly held assets have performed better so far. The switch changes the result, and when it is on the calculation runs twice and takes correspondingly longer.

corr.methodology_title: ℹ️ Methodology — what is measured here
corr.methodology_body:
- **Measure:** Pearson correlation of **daily log returns** (ln(C_t / C_t-1)), *not* of price levels or price trends. External tools/AI that instead compare price or trend paths can arrive at different values — up to the opposite sign (e.g. BTC/Gold: returns slightly positive, price trends can diverge).
- **Window:** rolling **30** or **90 trading days**. Shorter windows react faster and tend to run "hotter" than long ones for risk assets — compare magnitudes only within the same window.
- **Range:** −1 (perfect opposite) … 0 (decoupled) … +1 (perfect co-movement). Classification: |r|≥0.6 strong, ≥0.3 moderate, ≥0.15 weak, otherwise practically decoupled.
- **Instruments:** S&P 500 `^SPX`, Bitcoin `BTC-EUR` (proxy for BTC-USD — return correlation practically identical), Gold `GC=F`, US Dollar Index **`DX-Y.NYB`**, Copper `HG=F`, US Treasuries 10Y `ZN=F`.
- **Data:** local daily prices from the app database; recomputed daily by the scheduler. Other tools with a different data provider/snapshot or period will differ accordingly.
- **History:** the dollar index, copper and treasuries are only available locally from ~2024, so their curves start later.

gr.methodology_md:
**Global Rotation** shows where capital rotates between the major markets — as a **relative-strength proxy**, since actual fund flows (EPFR, ETF flows) are not available.

**Preparation:** each market index is converted to **EUR** via its FX pair (the currency move itself is part of the capital flow). The benchmark is an **equal-weighted EUR basket** of the markets themselves.

**Metrics** (identical to sector rotation):

- **RRG (Relative Rotation Graph)** — JdK RS-Ratio (x) and RS-Momentum (y). Each market rotates through four quadrants: *Leading* (strong & rising), *Weakening* (strong but turning), *Lagging* (weak), *Improving* (weak but rising). The tail shows the direction.
- **Mansfield RSC** — smoothed relative strength vs. the basket: positive = inflow proxy, negative = outflow.
- **Pair matrix** — relative strength market vs. market over several weeks: the concrete hand-offs (US↔EU↔JP↔HK).

**Sources:** index daily prices (`yf_^…`), FX pairs (`{CCY}EUR=X`, `EURUSD=X`, `GBPUSD=X`). Markets without an available FX series are skipped.

**Limitation:** relative strength is a proxy — outperformance can stem from earnings rather than flows; exact directed amounts are not measurable.

ma.howto_header: ℹ️ How to read these figures
ma.howto_body:
**Four of the five figures are coincident** — they describe where the market *stands*. Only the early warning looks ahead. The verdict (risk-on / neutral / risk-off) at the top is built solely from Fear & Greed, RRG quadrant and sector leader; correlation and early warning deliberately sit alongside it and *qualify* it.

---

**Fear & Greed** — sentiment index 0–100 from seven components. Extremes tend to act as contrarian signals: peak greed at tops, peak fear at bottoms. The direction (shown in brackets) matters more than the level.

**Rotation** — position of the home market in the Relative Rotation Graph against a EUR-normalised country basket. Rotation runs clockwise: Improving → Leading → Weakening → Lagging. "Improving" means still weaker than the basket, but gaining momentum.

*The country basket* holds eleven benchmark indices: United States (^SPX), Germany (^GDAXI), France (^FCHI), United Kingdom (^FTSE), Switzerland (^SSMI), Japan (^N225), Hong Kong (^HSI), Spain (^IBEX), South Korea (^KS11), Australia (^AXJO) and Brazil (^BVSP). Each is converted into euro at its exchange rate, reduced to weekly closes and rebased to 100 at the start of the comparison window. The basket is then the **equal-weighted average** of those eleven series, and relative strength is the ratio market ÷ basket.

Three properties worth knowing when reading it:

- **Equal-weighted, not by market capitalisation.** Australia counts as much as the United States. The basket therefore measures rotation *between* markets — it is not a world index and not an investable benchmark.
- **In euro, not in local currency.** A market can lead purely because its currency appreciated. For a euro-based investor that is the right measure: it is the return that actually arrives. Price action in local currency is what the index chart itself shows — the rotation hub works in euro throughout.
- **The home market is part of the basket** (roughly one eleventh). That dampens the swings — a market can never fully break away from its own yardstick.

The comparison window is the period *all* series cover, so the shortest one sets it — including when the gap sits in a market's EUR exchange rate rather than in the index itself. A market with less than about a year of weekly history drops out of the basket, and the composition changes silently.

**Equities↔Bonds** — rolling 90-day correlation of the **daily returns** of ZN=F (10-year US Treasuries) and ^SPX. Computed on log returns rather than prices — otherwise it would merely measure two shared uptrends. The values come from the nightly `recalc_correlation.py` run.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ≤ −0.20 | bonds cushion — the normal case, 60/40 diversifies |
| −0.20 … +0.20 | decoupled — both move independently |
| ≥ +0.20 | rate-driven — both hinge on the same factor |

At around +0.50 both mostly move in the same direction; roughly a quarter of the daily variation is shared. In practice: the bond cushion is not working, and a rate or inflation shock hits both sides at once. **Not a magnitude measure** — +0.50 says nothing about *how far* something moves, only how aligned the moves are. It is also a snapshot of the last 90 trading days, not a forecast; a change of sign is the informative event.

**Strongest sector** — highest Mansfield relative strength versus the reference index. Cyclical leaders (technology, banks, industrials) suggest risk appetite, defensive ones (utilities, staples, health care) caution.

**Early warning** — 0–100 from the breadth of the index members. The "price/breadth divergence" tag is the strongest warning: the index holds up or rises while fewer and fewer constituents follow. Lead time is days to weeks; false positives are possible and overnight or news shocks are not captured.

fps.method_md:
### The four phase sequence

**Phase 1 — proven history.** The stock produced at least one past up-leg above the threshold (default 90 %). Measured on monthly bars via a zigzag decomposition; a leg only counts once a counter-move has confirmed it, so nothing looks into the future. The benchmark index itself runs 60–90 % after bouncing off its 200-week SMA — an outperformer has to beat that.

**Phase 2 — consolidation base.** On weekly bars the longest sideways window is searched whose high/low range stays inside the base width and which sits near the 52-week high. Only names close to their record highs qualify.

**Phase 3 — breakout.** Close above the high of the completed base (plus buffer). That is the entry; the stop sits below the breakout or at the base low.

**Phase 4 — confirmed trend.** Price holds above the breakout level for a few weeks and above the rising weekly SMA. Positions are held until the close drops below the weekly SMA or the stop triggers.

**Exit.** Close below the weekly SMA (trend break) or below the stop. Optional trailing stop and profit taking at the target.

**Important:** every value is causal — base levels come from completed weeks, the Phase 1 history from confirmed monthly legs. The signals are therefore backtestable, not hindsight.
fps.integration_header: Use in Strategy Finder and Multi Strategies
fps.integration_md:
The method's columns are named identically live and in the backtest: `fps_phase`, `fps_buy`, `fps_sell`, `fps_base_high`, `fps_base_low`, `fps_stop`, `fps_target`, `fps_best_trend`, `fps_trend_gain`, `fps_rs`, `fps_dist_high`, `fps_breakout`, `fps_base_weeks`.

Enable the **fps** overlay in the Asset Viewer to see base, breakout, stop and target on the chart. The same columns work in buy/sell formulas (Strategy Finder, Multi Strategies), e.g. buy `(fps_buy > 0)` or stricter `(fps_breakout > 0) & (fps_rs > 0) & (fps_best_trend > 150)`, sell `(fps_sell > 0)`.

fps.columns_md:
| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Phase** | 0 no history · 1 watchlist · 2 base · 3 breakout · 4 trend |
| **Base (w)** | Length of the current sideways base in weeks. Empty = no valid base right now (too wide, too short, or too far below the record high). |
| **to breakout %** | How much the price still has to rise to take out the base high. 0.4 = 0.4 % below the trigger. Empty from phase 3 on — the breakout already happened. |
| **best trend %** | Largest **completed** past up-leg (monthly zigzag). This is the Phase 1 proof: what the stock managed before, the method expects it to manage again. |
| **running %** | The **current** leg: price against the last confirmed zigzag low. Compared with *best trend* it shows how much room this trend historically still has. While a stock is falling it measures the rebound off the running low. |
| **RS 52w (pp)** | Relative strength: own 52-week return minus the benchmark's, in percentage points. +30 = 30 points better than the index. |
| **Sector** | Sector from `asset_info`. |
| **vs. sector (pp)** | Own 52-week return minus the sector **median**. Positive = beats its own sector. Empty with fewer than 5 sector peers in the universe. |
| **Rank in sector %** | Percentile among the sector peers: 100 = best of the sector, 50 = exactly the median. |
| **off high %** | Distance to the highest close ever reached in the local history (**all-time high**), always ≤ 0. −5 = 5 % below the record. **Note:** the Phase 2 filter measures against the **record window** (10 years by default), not the all-time high — Commerzbank for instance sits 86 % below its 2007 high yet at a 10-year high, and therefore qualifies. |
| **Price** | Last close in quotation currency. |
| **Stop / Target** | Only with an open position (phase 3/4): stop = max(base low, breakout − stop percent), target = entry + target percent. |
| **last signal** | The method's most recent buy or sell signal, with date. |

The detail view shows the same figures as metrics — *best trend*, *running trend*, *RS 52w*, *off all-time high* and *vs. sector*.

fps.entries_header: Entry triggers: what actually works better
fps.entries_md:
The article buys the **breakout out of the base**. Measured over 656 index members since 2015 (same exit, same filters, signal to signal) there are two equal-or-better triggers — selectable under *Entry trigger*:

| Trigger | Trades | Win | Avg | PF | p.a. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base breakout (default) | 3,560 | 41.2 % | +6.5 % | 2.41 | +12.6 % |
| **New record high** | 3,053 | 42.3 % | +7.8 % | **2.59** | **+14.5 %** |
| New 52-week high | 4,175 | 41.3 % | +7.5 % | 2.52 | +14.4 % |
| Breakout **or** record high | 3,762 | 41.0 % | +7.2 % | 2.55 | +13.9 % |
| Retest of the broken level | 3,830 | 40.1 % | +6.2 % | 2.39 | +12.7 % |
| Reclaim of the SMA | 6,855 | 18.6 % | +1.4 % | 1.87 | +11.2 % |
| Pullback to the SMA | 11,023 | 21.1 % | +1.8 % | 2.03 | +12.0 % |

**Buying new highs is the strongest trigger** and beats the base breakout in all three sub-periods and both regions. The reason is plain: a name that marches straight up never forms the tight base Phase 2 demands — it would stay out of reach. Only 861 of about 3,000 entries are identical between the two, so *breakout or record high* takes whichever comes first.

**Waiting for pullbacks does not pay.** Buying at the rising SMA or after reclaiming it produces three times the trades at a ~20 % hit rate and short holds — that is a different strategy, not a better entry into this one.
fps.monthly_hindsight: The legs are **hindsight**: high and low are only fixed once the counter-move confirms them (✕ = that moment, typically 25–30 % below the high and months later). Buy and sell markers can therefore never sit on the leg ends — they only use what was known on the day. How close the entry gets to the start of a leg depends on the *entry trigger* (Method tab).

cand.method_md:
The chain runs from cheap to expensive — that is the reason for the order. Every step carries exactly one statement; the **direction** mirrors each direction-dependent one.

1. **Universe & prefilter** — the formula runs against the stored simulation data, one pass over every ticker. It takes the **most recent** row per ticker from the last ten days, not the most recent day overall: that one is often only partly computed. The default is deliberately direction-neutral and narrow — only volume and a band between support and resistance wide enough for a test of the level to mean anything.
2. **Tradable** — names marked as renamed or delisted drop out.
3. **Weekly trend** — the 4PS phases as a range: **3/4** requires the breakout to have happened, **2/3/4** adds the tight base, **1/2** looks only at what still has the breakout ahead of it. The phase survives a pullback; a momentum measure does not. Measured: COP sat in phase 2 on its reversal day, MDT in phase 1 — with 3/4 exactly the pullbacks one wants to buy drop out. There is no short counterpart (`fps_phase = 0` means "no proven history", not "falling"), so short uses `sma50 < sma200`.
4. **Level test** — who is approaching their support (long) or resistance (short), and who has returned to it after a break? Cheap and very selective, hence early in the chain.
5. **Sector with inflow** — keeps sectors showing relative strength (Mansfield RSC); for short, those with the strongest outflow.
6. **Pre-selection by strength** — the cut before it gets expensive, spread evenly over the qualifying sectors.
7. **Beats its own sector** — four-week return against the stock's own sector ETF. **Off by default**, and that is measured: a name testing its support is almost inevitably behind its sector — the step emptied the list completely in two runs. For a momentum selection it is the most useful step in the chain; for a pullback selection, the most harmful.
8. **Signal** — the short list through the same live path as the chart. That path is long-only, so for short the *exit* of the long strategy counts as agreement, which is a weaker argument than a real short signal.

Two things turned out wrong when measured, and they shaped the defaults: a momentum filter in the prefilter contradicts the pullback (`macd_trend_wk > 0` left 4 of 201 support tests, and none combined with `sma50 > sma200`), and `sup_support` is **not a fixed level** but a trailing floor — across some 150,000 rows the close sits below it in just two. A break is therefore measured against the *frozen* level from the start of the window; measured against the running one, every steadily falling name would look like one testing its support.

**The list is a shortlist, not a buy order.** It says which names are worth the analysis in the Asset Viewer.

cand.trend_mode_help: Measured structurally, not as momentum. A name falling back to its support has, by definition, no positive momentum — a momentum filter would empty the list (measured: 4 out of 201, and none when combined with sma50>sma200).

cand.retest_lift_help: How far the price must have been from the level within the window. Keeps out names that have been glued to it for weeks.

fund.method_sources: Source: “Statements” = computed from the four stored fiscal years. “Master data (TTM)” = a ready-made Yahoo figure for the trailing twelve months; more current than the statements, but it mixes quarters across the reporting date. “Statements + TTM” = computed from the statements with the TTM figure as a fallback (or the two combined). “Market + statements” = a market figure in the quote currency against a balance-sheet figure in the reporting currency — these are exactly the metrics that stay blank when the two currencies differ and no exchange rate is available.

fps.filter_setup_help: Keeps only candidates meeting at least this many quality criteria. Measured across 3,561 breakouts since 2015: score 0 → 38 % hit rate and PF 1.86, score 3 → 49 % and 3.37, score 4 → 52 % and 3.86. Only 15 % of breakouts reach score 3 or more — exactly the short list you want to see.
fps.setup_header: Finding candidates fast: the setup score
fps.setup_md:
Not every breakout is worth the same. Five features known **before** the breakout separate winners from losers across 3,561 breakouts since 2015. The **setup score** simply counts how many of them are met:

| Feature | Condition | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Short base | ≤ 12 weeks | 8–12 weeks: 48 % hit rate, PF 3.38 — 30–60 weeks only 38 %, PF 1.72 |
| Tight base | range ≤ 20 % | 10–15 % range: PF 3.26 vs 2.27 at 20–26 % |
| Rising trend | weekly SMA +5 % over 8 weeks | 47 % hit rate and PF 3.37 instead of 40 % / 2.19 |
| Lead | trigger ≥ 20 % above the SMA | 20–40 %: 49 % hit rate, PF 3.30 — just above the SMA only 36 % |
| Relative strength | RS 52w ≥ 20 pp | from +50 pp: avg +14.0 % per trade, PF 3.16 |

**Result, monotonic and stable across all sub-periods:**

| Score | Breakouts | Win | Avg | PF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1,611 | 38.1 % | +3.7 % | 1.86 |
| 1 | 944 | 40.0 % | +5.4 % | 2.14 |
| 2 | 458 | 42.6 % | +8.8 % | 2.86 |
| **3** | 309 | **48.9 %** | **+11.0 %** | **3.37** |
| **4** | 205 | **51.7 %** | **+17.1 %** | **3.86** |

**How to find candidates in a minute:** filter phase to *2 · base*, set *min. setup score* to 3 and “max. distance to breakout” to about 3 % — what remains are the names close to their trigger **and** carrying the favourable features. The table is already sorted by phase, score and relative strength.

What did **not** help: **volume** (higher volume was slightly worse) and the **size of the past trend** — a name with 4,000 % history does not break out better than one with 200 %.
